wstep: This card describes the NCHFP method for canning grapefruit sections, packed raw and covered with a hot light syrup, in a boiling-water bath.

akapity: Choose firm, mature, sweet fruit of a quality you would eat fresh.
NCHFP gives the recipe for grapefruit and orange sections and allows grapefruit to be canned without oranges; this card describes grapefruit only.
NCHFP uses on average 13 pounds (about 5.9 kg) of fruit for a load of 9 pint jars and 15 pounds (about 6.8 kg) for 7 quart jars.
NCHFP uses US measures: a cup holds about 237 ml.
Wash and peel the fruit, and remove the white tissue so the sections do not taste bitter.
NCHFP allows water, citrus juice or a very light, light or medium syrup; this card uses a light syrup.
Syrup helps keep the flavor, color and shape of the fruit, but it does not prevent spoilage.

For a light syrup (about 20% sugar) NCHFP uses 5 3/4 cups of water and 1 1/2 cups of sugar for a load of 9 pint jars, or 9 cups of water and 2 1/4 cups of sugar for 7 quart jars; heat the water and sugar together to a boil.
NCHFP gives only the raw pack for a boiling-water canner: the sections go into the jars raw.
Fill the jars with the sections and cover them with hot syrup, leaving 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) of headspace.
Put on the lids and process.
At 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) process pints or quarts for 10 minutes.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
At 1001–6000 ft (above 300 m up to 1800 m) process pints or quarts for 15 minutes.
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process pints or quarts for 20 minutes.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
NCHFP times are for US jar sizes: a pint holds about 473 ml and a quart about 946 ml.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): for a jar of up to 473 ml use the pint time, and for a larger jar of up to 946 ml, for example 0.5 l or 0.9 l, use the quart time.
This NCHFP recipe gives no time for jars larger than a quart, such as 1 l, so JarAtlas recommends smaller jars.
When you take the hot jars out of the canner, do not retighten the lids or bands; this can cut through the gasket and cause seal failures.
In raw-packed jars the food and liquid level will be noticeably lower after cooling.
If any jar loses a lot of liquid during processing, do not open it to add more.

Cool the jars at room temperature for 12 to 24 hours, then remove only the screw bands (the metal rings of two-piece lids), leaving the flat lids on the jars, and test the seal: press the middle of the lid, and if it springs up when you release it, the jar is not sealed.

This seal test and the whole method assume Mason-type canning jars with two-piece lids; NCHFP does not recommend jars whose mouths cannot be sealed with two-piece canning lids for canning any food at home.
A sealed lid is concave, curved down slightly in the centre; if the centre is flat or bulging, the jar may not be sealed.
If a jar has not sealed at this check, keep it in the refrigerator and eat it within several days.

Store sealed jars in a clean, cool, dark, dry place, not above 95 °F (35 °C) and not near hot pipes, a stove or a furnace, in an uninsulated attic or in direct sunlight; in such conditions the food may spoil.
Before using a stored jar, check that the lid is tight and holds a vacuum: a good seal has a concave centre.
Look for streaks of dried food running from the top of the jar, rising air bubbles and unnatural colour.
When opening the jar, check for an unnatural smell, spurting liquid and cotton-like mould on the food or under the lid.
Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or with signs of spoilage.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): throw out such a jar.
